_meta: A batch of A/A experiment results -- observed differences between two arms that were given the IDENTICAL treatment -- used to show why you run an A/A test to validate the whole measurement pipeline before trusting any A/B result: because the arms are the same, a correct pipeline should flag a significant difference only about alpha of the time (the false-positive rate), and a pipeline that flags far more than that is broken. An A/A test splits traffic exactly like an A/B test but serves both arms the same experience, so the true difference is zero and any 'significant' result is a false positive. Running many A/A tests (or one A/A test many times) and measuring how often the pipeline calls a difference significant is an end-to-end check of everything: the randomization, the metric definition, the variance estimate, the stopping rule. If that false-positive rate matches the alpha you chose (say 5%), the apparatus is trustworthy; if it is much higher, some part is wrong -- most commonly a variance estimate that is too small (treating correlated observations as independent, or using the wrong standard error), which inflates every test statistic and manufactures significance out of noise. differences is a set of observed A/A arm differences (centered near zero, since the arms are identical); se is the correct standard error of a difference; broken_se is the standard error a buggy pipeline uses (here, too small); alpha and its two-sided z critical value set the significance threshold. These are the fixture; each A/A test's z score and significance under the correct and the broken pipeline, and the two false-positive rates, are computed.
